text:
November in Slemani starts with a smell before it starts with weather: wood smoke, wet pavement, something roasting on a street cart.

Which smell tells you winter is close?
Kill List: this week we dropped a logo built around a mountain silhouette. Half the region already owns one. When the first idea in the room is the first idea everyone has, it's the first one we cut.

Before you ask any agency for a price, write one sentence: what should a stranger think about your business after five seconds?

That sentence shapes the whole quote. Send it to hello@33studio.org and we'll take it from there.
The dots in Kurdish script are small decisions with big consequences. Drop one, move one, and you've written a different word. Anyone who designs in this script learns to respect the dot.
A rebrand won't fix a business that treats people badly. It will just make the bad experience easier to recognise.

The first rain in Slemani turns every shop awning into a meeting point. Strangers, one metre of canvas, ten minutes of small talk.

The city designs its own social spaces when it has to.
Studio note: we spent an hour on one curve in one letter today. Nobody outside this room will notice it. Everybody will feel it.
Students: what's the one design rule a teacher gave you that you've since broken on purpose? Tell us below.

Three signs your brand has outgrown its look:

1. You explain your logo more than you show it.
2. Your staff design their own versions of it.
3. Your best customers describe you better than your sign does.

If that's you: 33studio.org

Kurdish is written in more than one alphabet depending on where you stand. Arabic script in Slemani and Erbil, Latin letters across the border to the north. One language, two very different shapes on the page.

That's a design brief nobody else in the world has.
“Make it pop” is not feedback. It's a feeling looking for a sentence. Ask the person what they want a customer to do, and you'll usually find the sentence.

Every neighbourhood in Slemani has one shop that has been there longer than anyone can remember. Same sign, same owner, same chair outside.

That's brand loyalty, and nobody had to plan it.
Open Desk: what did you make in October that nobody saw? Post it below. Unfinished counts.
Our sketchbooks have a rule: no erasers. If a line is wrong, draw the next one next to it. The mistakes stay on the page, and half the time the second line only exists because of the first.
A short thread on what a brand strategy actually is, for founders who've only been sold logos.
Strategy answers three questions before anyone draws anything: who you're for, what you stand for, and why someone should pick you over the shop next door.
It ends in a few plain sentences everyone in your company can repeat. Not a deck of 80 slides.
The logo, the colours, the voice and the website all come from those sentences. That's why they look like they belong together.
If you'd like those sentences written properly: 33studio.org
Tag a photographer from Kurdistan whose work you'd recognise without seeing their name. That's the highest compliment in this industry.
Design trends arrive in Kurdistan faster than ever. Our own visual history has been here the whole time and hardly anyone has borrowed from it yet.
A Kurdish wordmark next to an English one shouldn't look like a translation. It should look like the same person speaking a second language, with the same accent and the same confidence.

There's a particular blue painted on old doors and window frames all over the region. Nobody chose it from a swatch book. It's just what the shop had.

Some of the best colour decisions are accidents that lasted.

Your menu is the most-read piece of design in your restaurant. People hold it, study it, and argue over it. Most restaurants spend more on the chairs.

We design menus that sell the food. 33studio.org
Kill List: a campaign line that rhymed. It was catchy for one day and then it just sounded like a jingle. We'd rather be remembered for saying something true.
AI can give you a hundred logo options in a minute. Choosing the right one still needs someone who knows what the business is for. The hundred options were never the hard part.

Slemani at 5pm in November: the light drops behind the hills, the traffic thickens, and the tea glasses come out again.

What does your city look like at 5pm?

Branding your clinic? Patients read three things before they read your name: is it clean, is it calm, can I trust it.

Your sign, your forms and your waiting room all answer those questions. We design all three. 33studio.org
Calligraphers spend years learning a single stroke. Then a designer types the same letter in two seconds with a default font. Both have their place, but only one of them has a hand in it.
We present one direction, not ten. Ten options means we haven't done the thinking. One direction with reasons means we have, and it gives you something real to push against.
Open Desk: which shop sign in your city would you save if every sign had to be replaced tomorrow? Tell us where it is.
Who taught you to draw? A teacher, a parent, a cartoon on TV? Tell us below.
A good brief is shorter than a bad one. The bad ones list everything. The good ones say what matters most.

The pomegranate sellers have arrived. Red piled on red, on carts, in boxes, in plastic bags on every kitchen table.

Nobody ever ran a campaign to make this fruit the colour of autumn here. It earned the job by showing up at the same time every year.

Brief Clinic: “Make the Kurdish smaller so the English fits.” Rewrite: “Give both languages the space they need, and design the layout around that.” Two scripts on one sign is a feature, not a squeeze.

What to send us before a first meeting:

• What you sell, in one line
• A photo of your current sign, pack or page
• One brand you admire, from any industry

That's enough to start. hello@33studio.org

Studio note: someone asked why we still sketch on paper when everything ends on a screen. Because paper is fast and cheap, and you can throw it away without guilt. Good ideas need a place to be bad first.

Ask anyone who's tried: Kurdish text set right-aligned in software built for English breaks in odd ways. Punctuation jumps to the wrong end. Numbers flip. We test every layout in the real script, not in placeholder text.
Respect to the people who run printing shops in this city. They've fixed more broken files at midnight than any design school could teach.
If your brand only works on Instagram, it doesn't work. It also has to work on a receipt, a van, a uniform and a phone call.

Every old house in Slemani has a garden wall with something growing over it. Vines, roses, a fig tree that belongs to the neighbour.

Walk slower on the side streets. That's where the city keeps its best colours.

Launching a product? The packaging is your first salesperson and works every shift. It has about three seconds on a shelf to explain itself.

We design packs that win the three seconds. 33studio.org

Kill List: a colour palette we loved for a client in hospitality. On screen it was warm. Printed on the actual menus under the actual restaurant lights, it went grey.

We test in the real world now, every time.
The letter ە carries a lot of Sorani on its back. It sits at the end of countless words. In a logo, a letter that frequent can be the anchor everything else hangs on.
Open Desk: show us your workspace. Desk, kitchen table, floor, café corner. No tidying first.
Copying a big international brand's look won't make a local business look international. It makes it look like it wishes it was somewhere else.

The bazaar in winter changes its soundtrack: fewer fans, more kettles, sellers calling out over the hiss of gas heaters.

What's your favourite corner of the bazaar?

A logo should pass three tests before you pay for it:

1. It's still clear the size of a fingernail.
2. It works in one colour.
3. You could describe it over the phone.

If yours fails one, we should talk. 33studio.org
Studio note: the best idea this week came from the person who usually stays quiet in meetings. We now go round the table before anyone senior speaks.
Calligraphers of Kurdistan: if you'd like your work seen by more people, post a piece and tag us. We'll share the ones that stop us scrolling.
“We want something timeless” usually means “we don't want to do this again in two years.” Fair. Timeless comes from a clear idea, not from playing it safe.

Thinking of a website? Write down the one thing a visitor must do on it: book, call, buy, visit. Every page should point at that one thing.

Most sites forget. We build ones that don't. 33studio.org

The first morning you can see your breath in Slemani, the whole city changes pace. Hands in pockets, tea held with both hands, everyone walking a little faster.

Winter has a typeface. It's condensed.

Your business card still does a job a website can't: it's the thing left on someone's desk after you've gone.

Make it worth keeping. We design small things with the same care as big ones. 33studio.org
Kill List: an illustration style we'd been polishing for weeks. It looked great alone. Next to the brand's photography it looked like two companies. One of them had to go, and it was ours.
Sorani has letters that Arabic doesn't: ڕ, ڵ, ێ, ۆ. Most fonts treat them as an afterthought, with the marks floating a little wrong. Kurdish readers notice every time.
A brand that tries to speak to everyone ends up whispering. Pick the people you most want to reach and talk to them like you know them.

Heaters on, windows fogged, a row of shoes by the door. Winter in a Slemani home starts the day the carpets come back down.

What's the first sign of winter in your house?
Open Desk: what's one piece of work from this year you're proud of? Post it. Big or small, paid or not.

Opening a café this winter? Decide what people should feel before they taste anything. Warm, quick, quiet, lively.

The sign, the cups, the light and the music all follow from that one word. Tell us yours: 33studio.org
Studio note: we printed a brand's new colours on twelve different papers today and taped them to the window. By the afternoon, eight were out. Screens lie about colour; daylight doesn't.
Kurdish calligraphy and Kurdish typography are cousins, not twins. One is made by a hand, once. The other has to work a million times at every size. Both deserve designers who know the difference.
Designers in Kurdistan: what's a project you'd do for free if someone asked? A school, a bakery, a festival? Tell us below. Some of the best briefs start as wishes.
Consistency is boring to the person doing it and reassuring to everyone else. Your customers aren't tired of your brand. You are.

Slemani's rooftops are a map of the last fifty years: water tanks, satellite dishes, a pigeon coop, a line of washing that never fully dries in December.

Look up on your walk today.
A thread for anyone hiring a designer for the first time.
Ask to see the thinking, not only the final files. Good designers can explain every choice in plain words.
Ask how many directions you'll see. More isn't better. One well-argued route usually beats ten guesses.
Ask what happens after launch. A brand is a system you'll use every day, not a file you receive once.
And ask who will actually do the work. Then talk to that person. We're happy to answer all four: hello@33studio.org
We name every project in the studio after a word from the brief that surprised us. It reminds everyone what the client really said, months later, when the brief is buried in an inbox.
Tag a design teacher who changed how you see things. They rarely hear it.
A Kurdish headline set in a strong condensed face can stop a street. Most brands here never try, because the font menu offers three Arabic options and none of them were drawn with Kurdish in mind.
Most rebrands fail before the designer starts, when the owner says “we'll know it when we see it.” You won't. Write down what it needs to do first.

There are more bakeries in Slemani than you can count, and somehow you only trust one. Ask anyone. They'll give you directions to it in great detail.

That's the loyalty every brand is after.

Social media eating your week? Most businesses don't need more posts. They need a system: a look, a voice, a few repeatable formats, and a calendar.

We build content systems that save time. 33studio.org
Open Desk: what's a sign, poster or pack from Kurdistan's past that deserves to be brought back? Describe it, or post a photo if you have one.
Kill List: a mascot. Everyone in the room liked it, which was the problem. It was friendly, safe and forgettable. The brand needed an edge, and the mascot was the opposite of one.
Being cheap is a position. Being expensive is a position. Being in the middle and unclear about it is the hardest place to sell from.

Snow on the peaks around Slemani and blue sky over the city. People stop on the bridge to take the same photo they took last year.

Some views don't need improving. They just need noticing.

Designing in two or three languages at once? Start with the hardest one, not the English. Fit the Kurdish first and the rest falls into place.

We design bilingual and trilingual brands from day one. 33studio.org
The beauty of Arabic script is in the joins. Letters reach for each other. A good Kurdish logo keeps those connections instead of chopping the word into separate blocks to look “modern”.
Studio note: we read the brief out loud before every review. It sounds obvious. It stops a lot of beautiful work that answers the wrong question.

Brief Clinic: “We need a logo by next week.” Rewrite: “We need people to recognise us on the street within a year. Where do we start?” The second brief gets you a brand. The first gets you a file.

Send us either. We'll help with the rewrite. hello@33studio.org
Who's the most interesting brand founder you know in Kurdistan who has never been interviewed? Tag them. We'd like to hear their story.
Your brand's colour isn't the one in your logo. It's the one people remember after they walk past. Those are not always the same.

Every winter the same tea house puts the same heater in the same corner, and the same men claim the same seats around it.

Rituals are the strongest design system a city has.

Year-end is the best time to look at your brand honestly. Line up everything: sign, cards, posts, packs, uniforms. Photograph them together.

If they look like five different businesses, that's the project for January. hello@33studio.org
We keep a wall in the studio for things we didn't design but wish we had. Cinema tickets, a shop bag from the bazaar, a matchbox. It changes every month.
Numbers in Kurdish texts can switch between Eastern Arabic and Western digits within one page, sometimes within one sentence. A good layout picks one system and sticks to it.
Open Desk: describe your city's design in three words. Not your favourite city. Yours.
Every company says it's different. Few can say how in one sentence. The ones that can usually don't need much advertising.

December in the bazaar: wool socks hanging like bunting, stacks of blankets in every colour, and a seller who insists the red ones are warmer.

He's wrong, but he's a good salesman.

Running a school or a training centre? Parents choose with their eyes before they choose with a brochure. Your sign, your uniforms and your gate say more about your care than any slogan.

We help institutions look like they mean it. 33studio.org
Kill List: a typeface we'd chosen for its elegance. At small sizes on cheap printing it fell apart. Elegant at 200 points means nothing if the price tag is in 8.

Most Kurdish shop signs mix three alphabets: Kurdish in Arabic script, English, and sometimes a Latin transliteration nobody agreed on. It's chaotic. It's also the most honest picture of the city's language.
To every freelancer in Kurdistan chasing an unpaid invoice this month: you're not difficult for asking. You're running a business.
Your logo isn't where your brand lives. It lives in what people say about you when you're not in the room.
The light in December comes in low and gold through the windows of every shop on Salim Street, around four in the afternoon. For twenty minutes the whole street looks lit for a film.

Want people to recognise your brand without your logo? Pick one thing and own it: a colour, a shape, a phrase, a way of photographing your product. Then use it everywhere for years.

We help brands find that one thing. 33studio.org
Studio note: we argued for forty minutes about whether a headline needed a full stop. It did. It sounds more certain with one.
What's a Kurdish word that has no good English translation? Share it below with what it means. We're collecting them.
A slogan everyone in the industry would approve of is usually a slogan no customer will remember.

Winter evenings in Slemani belong to the corner shops: bright, warm, open late, with a man behind the counter who knows everyone's order.

The best customer experience in the city has no app.
Open Desk: what's one thing you learned this year that changed how you work? One sentence. We'll read every reply.

Building an app? The design isn't the screens. It's the moments: the first time someone opens it, the first time something goes wrong, the first time they come back.

We design web and app experiences around those moments. 33studio.org
We start every naming project with a list of names we're not allowed to use. Usually it's longer than the list of good ones by the end of day one.

Long Kurdish names are a gift for logo designers: more letters, more joins, more rhythm to work with. Short English names get all the attention, but a long Kurdish name can carry an identity on its own.
Kill List, year-end edition: the ideas we dropped this year would fill a wall. A few were good. None were right. That's the difference we spend most of our time on.
The shortest days of the year in Slemani, and the shops stay lit longer to make up for it. Walk the bazaar after dark this week. The city looks like it was designed for this light.

Planning next year's marketing? Before the budget, write the one thing people should know about you by December. Then judge every post, ad and event against it.

We help brands write that one thing and build around it. 33studio.org

A year of drawing Kurdish letters taught us one thing above all: the script has more range than the fonts that carry it. Heavy, light, playful, serious. The letters can do it. The tools are catching up.
Most “new year, new look” rebrands are just restless owners. Change your look when your business has changed, not when the calendar has.

Year-end in the bazaar means everything is wrapped twice. Plastic bag, then another plastic bag. Nobody leaves without a little extra in the bag and a “come again.”

That line is the entire loyalty programme, and it works.
Studio note: our most-used tool this year was not software. It was a thick black marker. If an idea doesn't survive being drawn with it, it's too fussy to work at small sizes.
A thread for founders writing their first brief this January.
Start with the problem, not the solution. “People don't know we exist” is a brief. “Make us a TikTok” is an order.
Say who you're trying to reach. One kind of person, described like a real human.
Say what you'd count as success. A number, a feeling, a behaviour. Anything you can check later.
Say what you can't change. Budget, deadlines, the logo your father drew. We'd rather know now.
Then send it: hello@33studio.org
Tag someone who made Kurdistan's creative scene better this year. Not famous. Just good.
A good year in branding is when nobody notices your brand changed, but everyone notices it works better.
Open Desk: what do you want to make this year that you've never made before? Write it here, so we can ask you about it in December.
Reading Kurdish right-to-left means the eye starts on the right side of a poster. Most layouts copied from English templates put the most important thing on the left. The headline gets read last.

New Year's Eve in Slemani: fireworks over the hills, every phone pointed at the sky, and someone's uncle insisting the ones in his day were bigger.

Happy new year from the studio.

First week of the year is when people decide what to fix. If your brand is on that list, start with an audit, not a redesign. We look at everything you have, tell you what's working, and what isn't.

No jargon, no pressure. 33studio.org
We cleared the studio wall for the new year. Every pinned sketch from last year went into one box, labelled and kept. A year from now we'll open it and laugh at half of it.
Your competitors' branding is not your brief. Their branding is the reason you need a different one.
January in Slemani: the cold that gets into the walls, the gas heater that clicks three times before it lights, and the first glass of tea that makes it bearable.
A good Kurdish logo should still look right when the sign maker cuts it out of metal, paints it on a wall, or sews it on a cap. Script that only works on screen isn't finished.

A logo is a signature. An identity is the whole handwriting. Your logo, colours, type, photography and tone should be recognisable even when the logo is missing.

That's what we build. 33studio.org
Kill List: a launch video with a big drone shot of the city. Beautiful, expensive, and the same opening as a hundred other videos. We started on a close-up of hands instead. People remember hands.

Brief Clinic: “Make it modern and clean.” Rewrite: “Our customers think we're old-fashioned, and we want them to see we've changed without losing the ones who've been with us for years.” Now there's something to design.
Students in Kurdistan: if you could ask a working studio one question, what would it be? Ask it below. We'll answer the best ones this month.
Advertising that apologises for interrupting you is still interrupting you. Be worth the interruption instead.

There's a man in every Slemani neighbourhood who fixes everything: shoes, radios, umbrellas, zippers. His shop is a metre wide and his sign is handwritten.

Every word on it is true. Most brands can't say that.
Open Desk: post a photo of a sign, a door, a tile or a pattern from your street that you walk past every day. Let's see what Kurdistan looks like up close.

Your website's homepage has one job: tell a stranger what you do and what to do next, before they scroll. Most homepages bury both.

We design sites that answer in one screen. 33studio.org
Kurdish words on packaging are often tucked under the English, smaller and lighter. Flip it once and see what happens. Customers here read their own language first.
Studio note: we started a rule this month. Every presentation must include one slide called “what we got wrong.” Clients trust the rest more because of it.
Which café in your city has the best design? Not the most Instagrammed. The one that feels right when you walk in. Name it below.
A strong brand gives a business permission to be simpler. Fewer products, fewer messages, fewer excuses.

Snow day in Slemani. Schools close, kids take over the streets, and every corner shop sells out of the same brand of instant noodles by noon.

The city has its own rhythms, even in the snow.

Hiring us for a TVC? Before scripts and casting, we ask one question: what should someone feel in the last three seconds? Everything before it is built backwards from there.

From script to screen, or through AI TVC: 33studio.org
We print every logo we design at the size of a building and at the size of a stamp, in the same afternoon. If it only works at one, we keep going.
The letter ۆ looks like it's wearing a little hat. Designers who love Kurdish know these details are where a brand's personality can hide.
You don't need a bigger budget to look premium. You need fewer things, done properly. Premium is mostly about what you leave out.

Every Slemani taxi has a small personal museum on its dashboard: a string of beads, a photo, a plastic flower, a phone holder held on with tape.

The most personal branding in the city.

Running a real estate project? Buyers can't touch the building yet. The brand is the only thing they can hold. The name, the hoarding, the brochure and the sales office all have to feel like the life you're selling.

We brand places before they exist. 33studio.org
Kill List: a name we liked because it sounded good in English. In Kurdish, said fast, it sounded like something else entirely. We say every name out loud in three languages now, fast.
Open Desk: what's the worst feedback you've ever received on a design? Tell us below, and what you did next.
To the people who keep old Kurdish magazines, posters and record covers in a box at home: please photograph them. That's design history, and a lot of it isn't in any archive.
“Our customers are everyone” is the most expensive sentence in marketing.

Breakfast in Slemani in January is a negotiation: who goes out for bread, who makes the tea, who gets the last piece of cheese.

What's on your winter breakfast table?

Need motion for your brand? Start small: an animated logo, a few moving templates for social, a set of transitions. Used consistently, that kit makes everything look like it came from the same studio.

We build motion systems. 33studio.org
Kurdish handwriting is getting rarer as everyone types. Ask someone older to write their name for you and keep the paper. There's a font in every person's hand.
Studio note: someone new to the studio asked why we spend a whole day on the brief before we draw. By Thursday they had the answer. Day one saves week three.
What's a local brand that's quietly got better this year? Not louder. Better. Tag them.
A brand built on a trend has a shelf life. A brand built on a truth about you doesn't.

Want your social channels to look like one brand, even with three people posting? Build templates, write a short voice guide, and agree on what you never post.

We set up content systems your team can actually run. 33studio.org
The bazaar spice sellers measure with the same tin cups they've used for years. Nobody asks for grams. Trust is the unit.
Slemani in deep winter is a city of steam: kettles, bread ovens, soup pots, breath on cold glass. Everything warm gets louder.
Kill List: a poster with seven messages. The client wanted all seven. We printed it, stuck it on a wall across the street and asked people what it said. Nobody could tell us. It went out with one.

Is your logo older than your youngest employee? That's not a reason to change it. If it still works, keep it and modernise around it. If it doesn't, we should talk.

We'll tell you honestly which one it is. 33studio.org
Open Desk: if you could rebrand one public thing in your city, a bus, a park, a street sign, a government form, what would it be? Tell us why.
Most international brands arrive in Kurdistan with their name transliterated by whoever was available that day. The letters are correct. The feeling is lost. Transliteration is a design job.
Fast, cheap, good: you've heard you can only pick two. In branding, pick good first. Fast and cheap can be fixed later. A bad identity costs you every day it's on the street.
There's a rhythm to a Slemani bakery queue: the paddle in, the paddle out, the flatbread flipped onto the counter, the coins on the tin plate. Nobody talks, and nobody needs to.
We have one rule for every mood board: no images from other agencies' portfolios. Pull from streets, archives, nature, old packaging. If it's already a brand, it's already someone else's answer.
Illustrators of Kurdistan: post one piece in the replies. We'll follow everyone who does and share a few on our page this week.

Your shop front works 24 hours a day, even when you're closed. Most businesses spend more on rent than on the one thing that tells people what's behind the door.

We design storefronts and signage. 33studio.org
A single Kurdish letter, drawn big and with care, can be a whole identity. Plenty of famous English brands are just one letter. Our alphabet has more interesting shapes to choose from.
Brand awareness is a weak goal. Being known isn't the same as being chosen. Ask what you want people to do, not just what you want them to know.
The windows of Slemani's old tailor shops are a lesson in display: one suit, one shirt, one bolt of cloth. No sale sign, no clutter. Just confidence.
Studio note: we threw out a full week of work today. It hurt. It was also the right call, and the next version came in two days because the week taught us what not to do.
A thread on naming your business, from the people who've made long lists of bad names so you don't have to.
Say it out loud in every language your customers speak. Some names that look fine on paper sound wrong.
Check the domain and the handles before you fall in love. Heartbreak at the registration screen is common.
Avoid names that describe exactly what you do today. Businesses grow. Names should have room to grow with them.
And pick one you can say proudly on the phone, every day, for twenty years. Need help? hello@33studio.org
Who's a Kurdish musician whose album covers deserve more credit? Tag the artist and the designer if you know them.
Clients don't buy design. They buy the confidence that the decision is right. Explain your thinking and the design gets easier to sell.
Open Desk: what's a design job that doesn't exist in Kurdistan yet but should? Type designer, packaging specialist, archivist? Tell us.

Brief Clinic: “Can you make it go viral?” Rewrite: “We want the right five hundred people to remember us.” Nobody can promise viral. Being memorable to the right people is a job we can do. 33studio.org

Mixing Kurdish and English in one headline is risky. The two scripts sit at different heights and weights, and most designers just let them collide. Matching the weight and aligning the baseline makes them feel like one voice.
The hills around Slemani after a January snowfall: white ridges, dark roads, and a sky that looks freshly washed. From the right spot you can see the whole city's palette at once.

Your brand doesn't need to be everywhere. It needs to be consistent where it is. Two channels done properly beat six done badly.

We help brands choose where to show up, and how. 33studio.org
We sketch every brand's worst possible version first, on purpose. The tackiest, loudest, most generic. Then we know exactly where not to go.
The most underused design tool is the word no. No to the extra colour, the extra font, the extra slogan, the extra logo on the poster.

Slemani's best design archive is on the walls of its old barber shops: faded photos, framed hairstyles, hand-lettered price lists that haven't changed in years.

Which barber shop wall would you frame?

Opening a gym, a salon, a studio? Members come for results and stay for how it feels. That feeling is designed: the entrance, the music, the towels, the app, the way the staff answer the phone.

We design that feeling. 33studio.org
Much of Kurdish poetry was made to be recited. Some of the most beautiful lines look ordinary in the default font. Set them with care and the page starts to sound like the poem.
Kill List: an icon set we were proud of, until we noticed every icon had a slightly different stroke weight. Nobody else had spotted it. We redrew every one.
Respect to the sign makers of Kurdistan who still cut letters by hand. When they retire, a lot of craft goes with them. Tag one if you know them.
A brand that only looks good in the presentation was designed for the presentation. Show it on a muddy van, a receipt, a phone screen at night.

Ever wondered what AI can actually do for your business, beyond writing captions? We build AI workflows that save real hours: briefs, drafts, image prep, reporting.

Useful, not flashy. 33studio.org
Open Desk: what does spring look like in your town? Post a photo, a colour, a sound, anything. Let's build a mood board of Kurdistan in March.

The fruit and vegetable stalls of winter arrange their oranges in perfect pyramids. Someone stacks them that way every single morning before dawn.

That's craft, and nobody calls it design.
Studio note: we started timing our meetings. Most decisions happen in the first ten minutes. The other forty are people agreeing loudly.
Photographers: post your best photo of Kurdistan in winter below. Our favourites might become our next desktop backgrounds.
Kerning Kurdish isn't like kerning English. The joins do half the work and the gaps between words do the rest. Get the word spaces wrong and a sentence reads like a list.

Not ready for a full rebrand? Start with a brand refresh: tidy the logo, set the colours, choose the type, write a one-page guide. It's quicker, cheaper and often enough.

We'll tell you if it is. 33studio.org
Under the old arches of the bazaar, the shadows are sharp enough to draw. Light and dark, one step apart. Best seen around midday in winter.
We test every headline by reading it to someone who isn't paying attention. If it catches them anyway, it stays.

Your packaging gets photographed more than your ads. Every unboxing, every shelf photo, every gift. Design it like it's going to be shared, because it will be.

We design packaging for that moment. 33studio.org
Older hand-painted Kurdish signs often used a confident, chunky hand-painted lettering that you rarely see now. Somebody should study it before the last of those signs disappear.
